title: The flute and the song offerings
hook: a small reed flute, carried over hills, played by someone else's breath
carry: bhakti: we offer god what god gave first
tomorrow: God in the dust of the road

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Gandhi's Gita with the person of steady wisdom: the tortoise drawing in, the sea staying level while the rivers pour in.

A reed flute is a plain thing. A hollow stalk, a few holes, nothing inside. It makes no sound on its own; somebody has to breathe through it. In 1912, a Bengali poet came to London with English versions of his own songs. The Irish poet W. B. Yeats read them, wrote the introduction, and the book came out that year with the subtitle Song Offerings. The next year its author became the first writer from outside Europe to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. The poet is Rabindranath Tagore. The book is Gitanjali, and its first poem is about that flute.
screen: `A REED FLUTE MAKES NO SOUND ALONE.` → `1912: SONG OFFERINGS.` → `TAGORE'S GITANJALI.`

segments.voice: Here is how the first poem opens, in Tagore's own English: "Thou hast made me endless, such is thy pleasure. This frail vessel thou emptiest again and again, and fillest it ever with fresh life." Then the flute: this little reed has been carried over hills and dales, and thou has breathed through it melodies always new. The singer doesn't make the music. He's the instrument. That flips the title around. A song offering sounds like a gift a person makes and hands up to God. Here the songs were breathed in from the other side first, and what's offered back was given. That is the heart of bhakti, loving devotion. In the Gita, Krishna says: offer me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, with love, and I accept it. The leaf and the fruit were never ours to begin with. At home shrines and in temples, families offer food to God, then take it back as prasad: the same food, now a gift returned. Tagore's poem ends on hands: the infinite gifts come only on these very small hands, ages pass, and still thou pourest, and still there is room to fill. He never names a god here; some readers hear Krishna, always pictured with a flute. Either way the bhakti question for a gift you give today, a meal, a song, a day's work, isn't how much did I make. It's what was I given, that I'm handing back.
screen: `EMPTIED AND FILLED AGAIN.` · `THE SINGER IS THE FLUTE.` · `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.` · `PRASAD: THE GIFT COMES BACK.` · then, large: `WE OFFER WHAT WAS GIVEN.`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open in your lap, palms up: small hands. Breathe out fully, then let the next breath come in on its own, and notice that you didn't make it; it arrived. Now bring to mind one thing you'll give today, a meal, a song, a piece of work. If you pray, offer it in your own words to the one you pray to, as a gift returned; if not, just notice what in it was given to you first.
Tagore's Gitanjali. Song offerings from a poet who pictures himself as a flute: what he gives back to God was breathed into him first.
Your line: bhakti: we offer God what God gave first. Tomorrow, a temple with its doors shut. See you there.

howItsDone: Many Hindus offer food to God at a home shrine or temple and receive it back as prasad; Tagore's Gitanjali songs, first written in Bengali, are still sung at home, in schools and at gatherings in Bengal.

original.note: Bengali, the language Tagore wrote the songs in. The English edition's subtitle is Song Offerings.

trapdoor: what you thought: Gitanjali is a book of poems a man wrote to God.

what a scholar hears: the English Gitanjali calls itself song offerings, translated by the author from the original Bengali, so the English is Tagore's own prose version, not a word-for-word rendering.
